strengths: The paper addresses an important scalability bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: dense pixel-aligned representations and full multi-view token interactions. The proposed decoupling of image tokens from lower-resolution viewpoint tokens, together with per-view cross-attention followed by global self-attention, is a sensible architectural contribution with clear computational motivation.

The experimental evidence is broad and mostly convincing. Results are reported on RE10K, ACID, DL3DV, high-resolution DL3DV, and a wide-coverage DL3DV protocol, with consistent gains in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS over recent feed-forward baselines in the reported settings.

The method appears practically useful: it often uses fewer Gaussians, has lower Gaussian-generation time and memory, and scales to more input views and higher resolutions better than pixel-aligned or cost-volume baselines such as MVSplat and DepthSplat.

The ablations are meaningful. The paper studies model depth, iterative repeated cross-attention, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention, initialization choices, mini-batch cross-attention, and representation density, which supports the main design choices rather than relying only on leaderboard tables.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes many implementation details in the appendix, including optimizer, training schedules, tokenization, Gaussian decoding, camera normalization, and training hardware.
weaknesses: Several headline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. The strongest gains on RE10K and cross-dataset evaluation come from using 4 or 8 input views while several baselines use their standard 2-view protocol. The 2-view version is still strong, but the much larger margins partly reflect additional input information rather than architecture alone.

The term 'iterative refinement' is somewhat overstated. The model repeatedly applies transformer blocks with cross-attention to image tokens, but it does not render intermediate predictions, measure residuals, or use explicit feedback/gradients as optimization-based methods do. This weakens the conceptual claim that it mimics per-scene optimization.

Runtime and memory comparisons need more caution. Some timings exclude rendering, some use different GPUs, and training/inference comparisons involve 4090, A100, H100, and H200 hardware. This makes efficiency claims directionally plausible but not as cleanly quantified as the tables suggest.

Evaluation focuses primarily on novel-view rendering metrics. For a 3D reconstruction paper, there is limited direct evidence of geometric correctness, multi-view consistency, depth accuracy, or failure modes under pose noise, dynamic scenes, reflective regions, or sparse/wide-baseline extremes.

Reproducibility is moderate but not complete from the manuscript alone. The method requires large-scale training on many high-end GPUs, uses dataset-specific protocols and preprocessing, and some comparison details depend on unavailable official models or inherited protocols. Code/model release status is not established in the manuscript text.

The method still requires known calibrated camera poses, which is a significant practical limitation for large-scale raw video reconstruction. The paper acknowledges this, but the empirical evaluation does not quantify sensitivity to pose errors.

strengths: The paper addresses an important scalability problem in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: avoiding full attention over all multi-view image tokens while still using high-resolution visual evidence.
The proposed decoupling of viewpoint tokens from image tokens, followed by per-view cross-attention and global self-attention, is a sensible architectural design with clear computational motivation.
Reported quantitative results are strong across RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV, with improvements in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS and substantially lower Gaussian-generation time and memory in several settings.

The paper includes useful ablations on model depth, iterative cross-attention, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention, initialization, and mini-batch cross-attention, which support several core design choices.
The method is potentially useful in practice because it can produce more compact Gaussian sets and can scale to more input views than pixel-aligned or dense-volume baselines.
weaknesses: The main empirical comparison is substantially confounded by input-view count. Many headline gains compare the method using 4, 8, 11, 24, or 32 views against baselines using fewer or fixed protocol views, so part of the improvement may come from additional observations rather than the architecture itself.

The claim of iterative reconstruction is somewhat overstated. The method is essentially a stacked transformer with repeated cross-attention; it does not include the render-error-update loop or gradient-based feedback that motivates the analogy to optimization-based 3D-GS.

Speed and memory claims are not fully clean. Some measurements exclude rendering, hardware differs across tables, DepthSplat is sometimes OOM or run on another GPU, and GS-LRM results rely on unavailable official code/models. This weakens the strength of the efficiency comparisons.

The novelty is incremental relative to existing transformer reconstruction models, alternating attention designs, latent/viewpoint embeddings, and iterative refinement work. The combination is useful, but the paper does not fully separate what is conceptually new from engineering choices.

Reproducibility is limited by the large training requirements and incomplete specification of some evaluation/training details. The paper uses 8 H100/H200 training in places, several dataset variants, curriculum schedules, and finetuning protocols that would be difficult to independently reproduce without released code and exact splits.

Evaluation remains focused on posed novel-view synthesis benchmarks. The method requires accurate camera poses, and robustness to pose noise, dynamic scenes, real SfM failures, and out-of-distribution scene types is not studied.

Some ablations are supportive but not decisive: for example, the no-iterative-refinement variant changes the distribution of cross- vs self-attention layers, and the same-number-of-Gaussians comparison also changes input resolution and training hardware/batch constraints across methods.

strengths: The paper tackles an important scalability bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: full multi-view token attention and pixel-aligned Gaussian generation become expensive as image resolution and number of views grow. The proposed decoupling of compact viewpoint tokens from high-resolution image tokens is a technically sensible and useful design direction.

The architecture is coherent: per-view cross-attention injects image evidence, self-attention exchanges global multi-view context, token uplifting mitigates resolution mismatch, and mini-batch cross-attention addresses training cost. The method is well motivated relative to GS-LRM, MVSplat, DepthSplat, and LongLRM.

Empirical results are strong across several relevant settings. On RE10K, the 2-view model already improves over reported feed-forward baselines, while 4/8-view variants show large gains. Cross-dataset results on ACID and DL3DV are also consistently favorable, and the DL3DV high-resolution and wide-coverage experiments support the claimed scalability advantages.

The efficiency story is convincing at a practical level: the method uses fewer Gaussians in several comparisons, reports lower Gaussian-generation memory/time than DepthSplat on DL3DV, and provides training-time/memory/FLOP ablations for the mini-batch cross-attention variants.

The paper includes meaningful ablations on depth/layer count, iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention, initialization, and mini-batch attention. These ablations support that the main components contribute rather than the gains being attributable to a single incidental implementation choice.

The work is likely useful to the community because it offers a scalable architecture for leveraging more views without tying Gaussian count directly to input image resolution, which is a practical limitation of many current feed-forward Gaussian methods.
weaknesses: Some headline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. The largest RE10K gains come from using 4 or 8 input views while many baselines are 2-view methods; although this is part of the paper's scalability argument, the performance advantage partly reflects access to more observations. The 2-view setting is stronger than baselines but by a more moderate margin.

The term 'iterative refinement' is somewhat overloaded. The model stacks update blocks in a feed-forward transformer and does not perform explicit render-error-update optimization at inference, so the analogy to optimization-based 3D-GS should be framed carefully. The current wording occasionally risks overstating the connection.

Evaluation breadth is good but still centered on novel-view synthesis metrics for known-pose settings. There is limited analysis of geometric accuracy, failure modes, pose noise sensitivity, dynamic/non-forward-facing scenes, or behavior when view count becomes very large, despite scalability being a central claim.

Reproducibility is decent but not complete from the manuscript alone. Training requires substantial hardware, multiple GPU types are used across settings, some baseline numbers rely on unavailable code/pretrained models or different devices, and key details are deferred to supplementary material. Exact sampling protocols, optimization settings, and implementation details would need to be very clear for faithful reproduction.

The mini-batch cross-attention contribution is promising, but its evaluation is mostly internal to the proposed architecture. More analysis of when the structured sampling strategies fail, and comparison to alternative efficient attention mechanisms, would strengthen the claim that this is the best practical design.

The wide-coverage DL3DV comparison is encouraging but has mixed metric behavior: the proposed method improves PSNR/SSIM over LongLRM while LPIPS is similar or slightly worse in zero-shot cases. The paper should avoid presenting this as uniformly superior visual quality without nuance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: scaling multi-view reconstruction to higher resolutions and many views without producing image-resolution-tied redundant Gaussians.

The proposed design is technically plausible and coherent: compact viewpoint tokens decouple representation density from image resolution, per-view cross-attention injects image evidence at each layer, self-attention exchanges information across views, and token uplifting/mini-batch cross-attention target concrete computational bottlenecks.

Empirical results are broad and generally convincing. The method improves over strong feed-forward baselines on RE10K, ACID, DL3DV, wide-coverage DL3DV, and additional zero-shot settings, often with fewer Gaussians and lower reported latency/memory. The high-resolution DL3DV results and scaling to 40/48 views are especially useful evidence for the paper’s central claim.

Ablations support the main architectural choices: repeated image cross-attention, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, number of update layers, self-attention, and mini-batch cross-attention each receive targeted evaluation.

The paper includes useful implementation details in the supplement, including optimizer settings, training schedules, Gaussian decoding, pose normalization, and hardware/training regimes, which helps reproducibility relative to many papers in this area.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat overstated. The method is framed as mimicking optimization or feedback-driven refinement, but technically it is a stack of cross-attention/self-attention blocks over latent/viewpoint tokens, related to Perceiver-style latent bottlenecks and alternating attention designs. The gradient-descent interpretation is intuitive but not formally substantiated and should not be treated as evidence of optimization-like behavior.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled. Several headline gains use more input views than baselines, larger parameter counts, different training budgets, or different hardware. The paper does include some same-view and same-Gaussian comparisons, but the main tables mix settings in ways that make it hard to isolate architecture quality from extra context, scale, or compute.

Efficiency evidence is promising but unevenly reported. Inference time sometimes excludes rendering, hardware varies across tables, and some baselines are evaluated on H100 while others on RTX 4090 or with unavailable timings. A stricter wall-clock/memory accounting under identical hardware and including full pipeline costs would strengthen the scalability claim.

The geometric claims are only partially supported. Main supervision is rendering-based, depth evaluation uses a monocular pseudo-depth model rather than ground truth, and geometry benchmarks are relegated to supplementary material with some caveats such as downsampling ground-truth pointmaps. This leaves uncertainty about true 3D geometric accuracy despite good view synthesis metrics.

The method still assumes accurate camera poses and static scenes, and the authors acknowledge self-attention across viewpoint tokens as a remaining scaling bottleneck. These are material limitations for deployment in broader real-world reconstruction pipelines.

Reproducibility is not complete from the manuscript alone: code/checkpoint release is not specified, training requires substantial multi-GPU H100/H200 resources for some variants, and certain implementation choices such as mini-batch cross-attention sampling details and baseline re-training protocols would need careful code-level clarification.

strengths: The paper addresses an important scalability problem in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: existing pixel-aligned or full-attention models become expensive as view count and resolution grow. Decoupling compact viewpoint tokens from high-resolution image tokens is a useful architectural direction.

The empirical section is broad. The manuscript reports results on RE10K, ACID, DL3DV, undistorted high-resolution DL3DV, Tanks&Temples, Mip-NeRF360, plus speed and memory comparisons. This is more substantial than a narrow single-dataset evaluation.

The reported numbers are often strong: e.g., on RE10K the method improves from 28.65 PSNR in the 2-view setting to 31.57 PSNR with 8 views while keeping inference around 0.03s, and on DL3DV it reports better quality, fewer Gaussians, lower memory, and faster inference than DepthSplat in several settings.

The paper includes meaningful ablations for model depth, repeated cross-attention, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention, initialization, mini-batch cross-attention, number of Gaussians, view overlap, and high-view-count latency. These support several design choices.

The method is potentially useful: compact Gaussian generation with high-resolution visual conditioning could be practical for fast reconstruction and for post-prediction optimization, where the paper reports better quality-time tradeoffs than Long-LRM.
weaknesses: The central framing as 'iterative' or 'feedback-driven' is overclaimed. The model repeatedly applies learned cross-attention to fixed image tokens, but it does not render the current scene, compute reconstruction residuals, or use explicit feedback from the current 3D estimate as optimization methods do. The gradient-descent analogy is mostly interpretive rather than technically demonstrated.

The originality is moderate. The architecture is largely a transformer with per-view cross-attention followed by cross-view self-attention over compact tokens, plus token-resolution decoupling. These are plausible and effective engineering choices, but the manuscript sometimes presents them as a stronger conceptual departure than the actual mechanism supports.

Several comparisons are difficult to interpret fairly because the proposed method often uses more input views than baselines. On RE10K, the strongest numbers use 4 or 8 views while several baselines are standard 2-view methods; the paper does include a 2-view variant, but many headline claims benefit from additional evidence rather than only architecture.

Training and hardware budgets are not consistently controlled. Different variants use RTX 4090, H100, and H200 setups, different batch sizes, different iteration counts, and pretrained initialization/finetuning protocols. This makes efficiency claims less clean, especially when comparing training cost or model capacity.

Some baseline comparisons are incomplete or potentially fragile. GS-LRM timing is missing, some methods are closed-source or re-evaluated under different constraints, DepthSplat is evaluated on H100 when it OOMs on 4090 in one setting, and Long-LRM 16-view weights are unavailable. These issues do not invalidate the results, but they weaken the strength of the comparative evidence.

The ablation for 'w/o iterative refinement' is not fully isolating the claimed mechanism: replacing repeated cross-attention with one cross-attention plus many self-attention layers changes information access and architecture behavior, but does not specifically prove an optimization-like feedback process.

Geometry evaluation is not fully convincing. Depth quality is partly assessed against pseudo-depth from MoGe-2 rather than ground truth, and the manuscript itself acknowledges that rendering-supervised geometry may be weaker than explicit geometry-supervised methods. The geometry claims should therefore be treated cautiously.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives many implementation details, but large-scale training requires substantial hardware, multiple dataset preprocessing protocols, flash-attention variants, and external rasterization/post-optimization choices. Without released code/checkpoints, reproducing the main results would be difficult.

strengths: The paper addresses an important scalability bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: dense pixel-aligned or full multi-view attention architectures become expensive as view count and resolution grow. The proposed decoupling of compact viewpoint tokens from high-resolution image tokens is a sensible and useful design direction.

The architecture is technically coherent. Per-view cross-attention injects image evidence, self-attention exchanges global multi-view context, token uplifting partially bridges low-resolution scene tokens with high-resolution image tokens, and mini-batch cross-attention provides a practical efficiency knob.

The empirical results are strong across several settings. On RE10K, the method improves substantially over reported baselines, e.g. 28.65 PSNR with 2 views and up to 31.57 PSNR with 8 views, while using competitive or lower inference time. On DL3DV, the method reports better quality, fewer Gaussians, lower memory, and faster inference than DepthSplat and Long-LRM in multiple regimes.

The paper includes meaningful scalability evidence: high-resolution DL3DV at 512x960, wide-coverage 540x960 experiments, unseen longer-context view counts, memory/time comparisons, and a 256-view inference-time stress test where Long-LRM runs out of memory but iLRM still runs.

The ablations are useful and mostly well targeted. The paper isolates model depth, repeated cross-attention, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention, group attention, mini-batch cross-attention, and viewpoint resolution, supporting the main architectural choices.

The supplementary material gives many implementation details, including optimizer settings, training schedules, pose normalization, Gaussian parameterization, and dataset-specific protocols, which improves reproducibility relative to many papers in this area.
weaknesses: The central 'iterative refinement' framing is somewhat overstated. The model repeatedly applies learned cross/self-attention layers to fixed image evidence, but it does not render intermediate predictions, measure reconstruction error, or use actual feedback from the current rendered scene. This is a reasonable architectural analogy, but weaker than the optimization-like interpretation repeatedly emphasized in the manuscript.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled for input information. On RE10K and cross-dataset generalization, the strongest iLRM numbers use 4 or 8 input views while several baselines are primarily compared in their standard 2-view setting. The paper does include same-Gaussian and other supplementary comparisons, but the headline performance gains partly conflate architecture with access to more views.

The evaluation relies heavily on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS novel-view synthesis, and the main paper has limited direct evidence of geometric correctness. Supplementary geometry results help, but pseudo-depth evaluation using MoGe-2 is only an indirect proxy, and more ground-truth geometry evaluation would strengthen claims about 3D consistency.

The computational efficiency claims are generally convincing, but hardware and implementation conditions vary across tables: RTX 4090, H100, H200, FlashAttention v3, closed-source methods, unreleased 16-view Long-LRM weights, and occasional OOM handling. This makes some speed and memory comparisons less clean than the narrative suggests.

The method still requires accurate posed multi-view input and is limited to static scenes, which the authors acknowledge. Robustness to pose noise is tested only for translational perturbations in the supplement, leaving practical behavior under realistic pose errors and rotations underexplored.

Reproducibility remains nontrivial despite detailed hyperparameters because the method requires large-scale training on 8 H100/H200 GPUs for key settings, multiple dataset variants, and some comparisons to closed-source or externally checkpointed baselines. The manuscript does not make clear whether code and pretrained models will be released.
